item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note1: Burn seashells or white stone and you get lime: the start of wall plaster.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note: CaO. Calcite (CaCO3) heated to about 900 C loses its carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. A furnace (~1000 C) or blast furnace is hot enough. Seashells and limestone are also CaCO3 and burn the same way.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note3: Lime plaster is one of the oldest man-made materials: floors at Catalhoyuk and other early villages (around 9000-7000 BC) were coated with burnt lime. People built lime kilns everywhere there was limestone or shells.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.note4: Above about 900 C the pressure of CO2 released by CaCO3 exceeds 1 atm, so the reaction runs on its own. Burned too hot or too long, lime becomes 'dead-burned' (dense crystals that react slowly with water). The CO2 from lime kilns is still a big part of the cement industry's emissions.
item.semiconductor-lab.quicklime.placeho: Omitted: the CO2 given off is not collected (a furnace has only one output).
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note1: Pour water on quicklime and it gets hot enough to steam, then falls into a white powder.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note: Ca(OH)2. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 gives off a lot of heat. Mixed as 'milk of lime' (about 2%), it binds silica sand into Dinas refractory bricks. In air it slowly takes back CO2: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, which is how lime plaster hardens.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note3: The Romans mixed slaked lime with volcanic ash (pozzolana) and got a concrete that sets even under water. Japanese castle walls (shikkui plaster) are slaked lime with seaweed glue and fibres.
item.semiconductor-lab.slaked_lime.note4: Slaking releases about 65 kJ per mole of CaO, enough to boil water or set wood on fire; self-heating meal boxes still use this reaction. Slaked lime is a strong base (pH about 12.4) used to causticize potash [2-02] and soda [2-08] and to neutralize acids.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note1: The bitter liquid left after boiling seawater. It sets tofu.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note2: Nigari: the mother liquor left after NaCl crystallises from boiled seawater. Mostly MgCl2 (plus MgSO4, KCl). Future raw material for magnesium [1-39].
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note3: Seawater is about 3.5% salt. When you boil it down, NaCl crystallises first and magnesium salts stay in the liquid. That bitter liquid is nigari, the traditional coagulant for tofu.
item.semiconductor-lab.bittern.note4: From 1941 Dow Chemical made aircraft magnesium from seawater in Freeport, Texas: Mg(OH)2 precipitated with lime, dissolved in HCl, then molten MgCl2 electrolysed. 1 L of seawater holds about 1.3 g of Mg.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note1: Makes salt from seawater using the sun. Put it on the beach next to water.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note2: Works only in ocean/beach biomes, with water beside it, open sky above and no rain. Makes 1 salt per minute and 1 bittern per 8 salt. Right-click to collect (holds up to 64 salt / 16 bittern).
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note3: Agehama style: seawater is sprinkled on a sand bed, the sun dries it, the salty sand is washed to get strong brine (kansui), then boiled down in a pot. Noto in Japan still does it this way.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.note4: Salt-making pottery from the late Jomon period has been found in Japan. In the Edo period the Seto Inland Sea used tidal 'irihama' pans. Since 1972 Japanese salt has been made by ion-exchange membrane electrodialysis instead.
block.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.placeho: Approximation: the fuel for boiling down the brine is skipped (it runs on sunshine alone).
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.worki: Salt pan: drying in the sun (%s%%)
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.not_s: Salt pan: not by the sea (needs an ocean or beach biome)
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.no_wa: Salt pan: no seawater beside it
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.no_sk: Salt pan: no sunlight (needs open sky above)
message.semiconductor-lab.salt_pan.full: Salt pan: full - right-click to collect
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note1: A round, hard river pebble. Strike flint with it and sharp pieces fly off.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note2: Sometimes found when breaking gravel. Right-click with flint in the other hand to knap 2 flakes. Right-click an obsidian block for an obsidian flake (the block stays). Ordinary stone will not give an edge. Returned when used in crafting.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note3: Striking stone with stone (direct percussion) is humanity's oldest technology. The oldest secure examples are Oldowan tools from Gona, Ethiopia, about 2.6 million years old. Tools from Lomekwi, Kenya, are dated to about 3.3 million years, but their age and whether they were made on purpose are still debated ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.note4: Knappers chose tough, hard-to-break hammerstones (quartzite or basalt cobbles). The striking angle (less than 90 degrees between platform and edge) and the spot matter: a good blow spreads as a cone of force (a Hertzian cone) and detaches a flake, leaving a bulb of percussion on its inner face.
item.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.place: Omitted: flake size, striking angle and failed fractures. The hammerstone comes from gravel (really you pick a rounded river cobble).
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note1: Hit a stone with a stone and it breaks with a knife-sharp edge. Humanity's first blade.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note2: Knap flint with a hammerstone (right-click or crafting table, 1 flint -> 2 flakes). A small blade for cutting and fighting. No handle, so it wears out fast. Repair with flint or obsidian.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note3: Flint is made of extremely fine quartz (SiO2) grains, so it breaks like glass with a conchoidal (shell-like) fracture and a razor edge. The Oldowan toolkit (about 2.6 million years ago) is just such flakes plus the cores they came from. Silicon for chips is made from the same SiO2.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.note4: Cut marks on animal bones show what Oldowan flakes (named after Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania) were for: stripping meat and cracking bones for marrow. Oldowan tools about 2.9 million years old have been reported from Nyayanga, Kenya ⚠️.
item.semiconductor-lab.flint_flake.place: Omitted: different flake tools (scrapers, points) are merged into one item.
item.semiconductor-lab.obsidian_flake.no: A flake of volcanic glass. Extremely sharp, but brittle.
Right-click an obsidian block with a hammerstone (the block stays). Sharper than a flint flake but chips quickly (half the durability).

Obsidian is natural glass: lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. With no grains, its fractured edge is only a few nanometres thick, sharper than a steel scalpel. In Palaeolithic and Jomon Japan, obsidian from Wada Pass (Nagano) and Kozushima island travelled far.

Kozushima obsidian was carried across the sea to Honshu from around 38,000 years ago ⚠️. Obsidian blades are still used in some surgery. In 19th-century Australia, Aboriginal knappers made beautiful Kimberley points from discarded bottle glass: natural or man-made, glass breaks the same way.
item.semiconductor-lab.obsidian_flake.pl: Omitted: the obsidian block is not used up (one block counts as a big raw nodule).
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note1: A teardrop-shaped stone knapped on both faces. No handle: you grip it in your hand.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note2: 3 flint + hammerstone (returned). Works as an axe (a little faster than a wooden axe, but swings slowly without a handle). Repair with flint or obsidian. The vanilla stone axe is the later hafted stone tool.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note3: The hand axe is the signature tool of the Acheulean (named after Saint-Acheul, France). It appeared in Africa about 1.7 million years ago and was made in nearly the same shape for over a million years. Knapping both faces symmetrically needs a picture of the finished tool in the maker's mind.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.note4: The oldest Acheulean tools come from Kokiselei, Kenya (about 1.76 million years) and Konso, Ethiopia (about 1.75 million years). Hafting a stone point onto a wooden shaft is thought to date from about 500,000 years ago (Kathu Pan, South Africa) ⚠️; vanilla stone tools (cobblestone + stick) correspond to that stage.
item.semiconductor-lab.hand_axe.placehol: Omitted: the second, shaping stage with a soft hammer (bone or wood).
message.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.gl: Crack! Glassy stone breaks like a shell - you got a sharp flake
message.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.gr: Thud... Coarse-grained stone just crumbles along its grains. No edge
message.semiconductor-lab.hammerstone.fl: Clink! You knapped 2 flakes from the flint
